extracted.intended_audience: criminalists, trial judges, prosecutors, defense counsel, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for legal practitioners on interpreting and applying notions of probability, chance, rules, and persuasion in criminal procedure — including how to evaluate evidence, avoid statistical and logical mistakes, and present evidence persuasively to juries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between demonstrable and probable knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a sharp distinction between demonstrable (certain) and probable knowledge; classify fundamentals as evidence, certainties, and probabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certainties are fundamentals supported by experience and leave no room for doubt; probability is a lower degree of certainty (Laplace, Mill); the practitioner should mentally separate evidence that is demonstrative from that which is only probable when judging cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditioned vs. unconditioned probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate conditioned probability (based on the specific conditions of the case) from unconditioned (statistical) probability derived from general observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditioned probability depends on present, case-specific conditions (e.g., weather measurements, evidence context) and must be calculated from relevant antecedent facts; unconditioned probability uses past statistics (e.g., proportion of solved murders over ten years) and must not be substituted for or double-counted with conditioned probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of double-counting probability evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not count the same probabilistic factor twice by conflating conditioned and unconditioned probabilities or treating one factual basis as two separate supports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: combining a conditioned inference (manner of crime suggests a thief) with an unconditioned statistical tendency of thieves to reoffend can mistakenly produce two seemingly independent reasons when they are the same probability counted twice; this leads to erroneous strengthening of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of types of probability (general, inductive, mathematical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize Kirchmann's subdivision: (1) General probability (depends on causes/consequences), (2) Inductive probability (from single events to universals), (3) Mathematical probability (arithmetical counting of equally possible cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For criminalists the first two forms (general and inductive) are of equal importance; mathematical probability is rarely of value in practice because true arithmetical cases are uncommon and it is of transitory worth unless it leads to actual counting of cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites for applying statistical/mathematical probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Before applying probabilistic calculations, know the necessary facts: the relative frequencies of events and the causes that produce them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill's counsel: statistical tables justify inference only when the observer understands how often events occur and why; use statistics only when their presuppositions (constancy of conditions, independence) hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of constancy of general conditions for valid probabilistic rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical rules of probability are valid only when the constancy of general conditions and independence of events can be reliably assumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kries warns that applying probability calculus where presuppositions fail (e.g., mortality data, witness statements) produces delusory results; check that observed series genuinely conform to the assumptions of the probabilistic schema.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward numerical precision and overreliance on figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about exact-looking figures and round numbers; human reporting habits and rhetorical aims often corrupt statistical appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People invent irregular specific numbers to appear precise; suspiciously neat or repeated proportions (e.g., identical jury vote splits occurring repeatedly) may indicate error or manipulation; do not overvalue figures without examining their provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of generalization and the unreliability of 'rules'
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat 'rules' as customary recurrence (regularity) rather than inviolable natural laws; avoid premature generalization without investigating possible exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalizations become dangerous when exceptions are overlooked; verify who established the rule, how broad the observation was, and whether exceptions would have been noticed (Mill, Schiel, Lotze). Do not assume a rule without testing its basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper interpretation of others' assertions of generality ('always' claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: When someone asserts 'this is always so', examine the methods: who counted, what precautions were used, and whether exceptions were sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept blanket statements at face value; the interpreter must investigate the determining conditions and the care taken to avoid overlooking exceptions before relying on such assertions in inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate role of probability in procedural thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Where law calls for 'a definite degree of probability' (preliminary examinations, arrests, investigations), require that the event appear true though not proved; nothing must exist to destroy appearance of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law does not quantify required probability; practitioners should stick to the notion that the event must appear true as far as possible; balance caution with the practical needs of procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of possibility separate from probability in procedural design
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that many procedural institutions are based on possibility (not just probability): appeals assume possible incorrect judgments; exclusions assume possible prejudice; publicity assumes possible incorrectness, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or designing procedural safeguards, treat possibility (risk of error, prejudice, or omission) as distinct from statistical likelihood and ensure measures address these possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish chance (accident) from causal relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a combination of circumstances indicates a causal relation to the crime or is merely accidental coincidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal fact-finders must seek causal relations and beware of mistaking 'unfortunate coincidence' for causation; when laws linking events are unknown, interpret combinations cautiously under the maxim 'simul cum hoc non est propter hoc'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative and knowledge-dependent nature of chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that what is called 'chance' is relative to the observer's knowledge: an event may be accidental for one perspective but lawfully explicable from a broader perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions of chance vary (Aristotle, Kant, Quetelet, etc.); practical treatment requires gathering rich casuistry and searching for hidden laws before concluding an event is accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arranging facts dishonestly or selectively to achieve a favored conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not arrange or group facts in a way that produces a sophistical or biased conclusion; honest study should reveal how many possible conclusions may be drawn from the same facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sophistical dialectic can make numbers 'prove' different things by re-arrangement; the examiner should present facts objectively and consider alternative arrangements and conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize suggestive eloquence when examining witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should meet witnesses with the least conceivable use of eloquence to avoid persuading or leading them into adopting the examiner's point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witnesses can be unintentionally persuaded by the examiner's manner or phrasing and may later believe they hold those thoughts independently; avoid suggestive questions and excessive eloquence—especially with lay witnesses who are more easily influenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art of drafting the brief: ordering evidence for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a case intelligible, the criminalist must determine the chronological order and logical sequence in which to present evidence (the 'brief'); good ordering makes the case develop logically and psychologically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor or irrelevant ordering will leave juries unable to follow; crafting the brief is an 'artistic' and demanding task—when done well it shapes jury understanding; when poorly done, even strong evidence may fail to persuade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and counteract jury susceptibility to rhetorical persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that juries are especially influenced by oral addresses; persuasive speech often substitutes for detailed comprehension of testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For juries, the prosecutor's or defense's orations can dominate verdicts because jurors rely on those summaries to make sense of evidence; presiding judges should observe jurors' reactions and act as psychologists to mitigate undue rhetorical sway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-awareness about the examiner's tendency to assume others share expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume that witnesses, defendants, or lay observers possess the same knowledge, acuteness, or perspectives as the criminalist; be wary that the examiner may overestimate how 'obvious' conclusions are to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practitioner often takes his or her hard-earned convictions for granted; remind yourself that others may not see the case the same way and avoid imposing your perspective on them through conduct or questioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expert institutions grounded in probabilistic trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that institutions such as expert testimony, oaths, or warrants rest on probabilistic assumptions (experts probably make no mistakes; witnesses tell truth under oath; warrants likely reveal evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these institutional trusts as reasoned probabilities that can be challenged—do not accept institutional assumptions as proof beyond scrutiny.
